```{r}
#| label: seasonal-ne-table
if (exists("temporal")) {
  temporal %>%
    transmute(Clade = clade, Pair = pair, Generations = gens, SNPs = snps,
              Fc = round(Fc, 3), `Excess (calibrated)` = sprintf("%.4f ± %.4f", excess, se),
              Ne = if_else(is.finite(ne), sprintf("%.0f", ne), "∞"),
              `Ne 95% CI` = sprintf("%.0f – %s", ne_lo, if_else(is.finite(ne_hi), sprintf("%.0f", ne_hi), "∞"))) %>%
    knitr::kable(caption = "Temporal F~c~ and N~e~ per seasonal pair, with sampling noise calibrated by the split-half c. CI from a delete-one-chromosome jackknife of the excess; ∞ = excess not distinguishable from zero.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-parallel
if (exists("temporal")) {
  # parallel change: correlation of early→peak changes between X sites
  mx <- read_tsv(cx("results", "09_stage34", "X.freqs.unlinked.tsv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(chrom = "c"))
  dp <- function(site, s1, s2) {
    a <- paste0("X__", site, "__", s1); b <- paste0("X__", site, "__", s2)
    ok <- mx[[paste0("nind_", a)]] >= 5 & mx[[paste0("nind_", b)]] >= 5
    if_else(ok, mx[[paste0("freq_", b)]] - mx[[paste0("freq_", a)]], NA_real_)
  }
  d <- tibble(chrom = mx$chrom, ME = dp("ME", "early", "peak"), TK = dp("TK", "early", "peak"),
              RW = dp("RW", "early", "peak")) %>% drop_na()
  par_tab <- map_dfr(list(c("ME", "TK"), c("ME", "RW"), c("TK", "RW")), function(p) {
    r <- cor(d[[p[1]]], d[[p[2]]])
    jk <- map_dbl(unique(d$chrom), function(ch) { k <- d$chrom != ch; cor(d[[p[1]]][k], d[[p[2]]][k]) })
    g <- length(jk)
    tibble(comparison = paste(p, collapse = " vs "), snps = nrow(d), r = r,
           se = sqrt((g - 1) / g * sum((jk - mean(jk))^2)))
  })
  knitr::kable(par_tab, digits = 3,
               caption = "Clade X: correlation of early→peak allele-frequency change between sites (unlinked SNPs; SE from a delete-one-chromosome jackknife)")
}
```

Calibration removes almost all of the apparent excess: with two chromosomes per individual assumed, every pair showed an excess of ≈ 0.05 regardless of the number of generations (open circles); with the calibrated sampling term the excess is 0.000–0.011 (filled points). Most pairs give N<sub>e</sub> in the high hundreds to a few thousand, with lower 95% bounds of roughly 400–2,000, and several upper bounds are infinite (no drift detectable within the season). These estimates describe drift over a few to ~20 generations within one season, not long-term N<sub>e</sub>, and they are at or above the lab estimate of ~400. ME early→peak is the exception (N<sub>e</sub> ≈ 225, CI ≈ 185–285): ME early is the smallest X sample (10 individuals), so a modest error in its c would inflate the excess, and the value should be checked before it is interpreted biologically. In clade X, early→peak changes at different sites remain uncorrelated genome-wide (r ≈ 0).

**Per-SNP seasonal test.** For each SNP, the minor-allele count was modelled with a binomial GLM, count ~ site + x, with each population weighted by its effective number of chromosomes (2cn), as in the *Drosophila* seasonal studies ([Bergland et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1004775); [Machado et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.67577)). Two versions of x were fitted: (1) **time**, the collection day of year scaled from 0 (first sampling event at a site) to 1 (last), which rewards change in the same direction through the season at every site; and (2) **temperature**, the mean MUR SST over the generation before each collection (Ganey's Wharf corrected against station ET5.1), which rewards change that tracks temperature, so that a warming and a cooling step move frequencies in opposite directions. Temperature matters because the season is not a monotonic temperature ramp: water before the early and peak collections was similar (or cooler at peak in the north), and the late collections followed a strong cooling. The null distribution comes from permuting x among each site's sampling events, enumerating every distinct ordering (time: X 11 and F 23 permutations, as reversing all sites only flips the sign; temperature: X 23 and F 47). The genome-wide test asks whether more SNPs reach a given p value with the real values than with the permuted ones. Results are shown with and without chromosome 6, which carries the likely inversion in clade X (Section 3.2). Clade S has a single seasonal site (MD) with two samples, so it has no permutation null and is not shown.

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-glm
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
glm_files <- c(Sys.glob(cx("results", "13_seasonal", "*.perm.tsv")),
               Sys.glob(cx("results", "13_seasonal", "temp", "*.perm.tsv")))
if (length(glm_files) == 0) {
  cat("Seasonal GLM results are not in this export yet.")
} else {
  glm_perm <- map_dfr(glm_files, function(f) {
    read_tsv(f, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(clade = str_split_1(basename(f), "\\.")[1], snps_used = str_split_1(basename(f), "\\.")[2],
             model = if_else(basename(dirname(f)) == "temp", "temperature", "time"))
  }) %>%
    filter(clade %in% c("X", "F")) %>%
    mutate(snp_set = if_else(snp_set == "all", "all chr.", "no chr6"),
           model = factor(model, levels = c("time", "temperature")),
           panel = paste0(clade, ", ", snps_used, " SNPs"),
           clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)) %>%
    pivot_longer(starts_with("n_p<"), names_to = "threshold", values_to = "n_snps") %>%
    mutate(threshold = sub("n_", "", threshold), observed = perm == 0)

  glm_perm %>%
    filter(threshold %in% c("p<0.01", "p<0.001"), snp_set == "all chr.") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = model, y = n_snps)) +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, !observed), colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.7,
               position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, observed), aes(colour = clade), size = 3.5, shape = 18) +
    facet_wrap(threshold ~ panel, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = clade_cols[tonsa_clades], guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "SNPs below threshold",
         caption = "Diamonds: observed. Grey: every within-site reordering of the sampling events. All chromosomes (with/without chr6 in the table).") +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 11)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-glm-table
if (length(glm_files) > 0) {
  glm_perm %>%
    group_by(clade, snps_used, model, snp_set, threshold) %>%
    summarise(obs = n_snps[observed], perm_mean = mean(n_snps[!observed]),
              perm_max = max(n_snps[!observed]),
              rank = sum(n_snps[!observed] >= n_snps[observed]) + 1, label_sets = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(rank = paste0(rank, " / ", label_sets)) %>%
    select(-label_sets) %>%
    arrange(clade, snps_used, model, snp_set, threshold) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 1, col.names = c("Clade", "SNPs", "Model", "Chromosomes", "Threshold", "Observed",
                                          "Permutation mean", "Permutation max", "Rank of observed"),
                 caption = "Per-SNP seasonal GLM: SNPs below each p threshold with the real seasons vs all within-site permutations (rank 1 = more than every permutation).")
}
```

There is no genome-wide excess of seasonal SNPs in either clade, with either model. With the real seasons, X and F have about as many low-p SNPs as the permuted orderings, at every threshold, on both the unlinked and the full SNP sets. Modelling temperature instead of time does not change this: the closest to a signal is clade X on all SNPs (rank 5–6 of 24 at p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, i.e. p ≈ 0.2–0.25), which is not significant and does not hold on the unlinked set. Removing chromosome 6 changes nothing, so the X inversion is not driving or masking a seasonal signal. The genomic-control λ is close to 1 (X ≈ 1.1, F ≈ 1.0) for the observed and permuted values alike, so the calibrated binomial weights describe the sampling variance well. Together with the uncorrelated early→peak changes across X sites, this means that any seasonal selection in these populations acts on too few loci, or is too weak, to show up genome-wide with 3–4 seasonal sites per clade, whether it is modelled as a seasonal trend or as a response to temperature. Individual SNPs with the smallest p values are listed in `results/13_seasonal/*.top.tsv` and `results/13_seasonal/temp/*.top.tsv` but are not more numerous than expected by chance, so none can be called a seasonal candidate on its own. The permutation null is coarse (time: 12 and 24 orderings; temperature: 24 and 48), which limits the smallest attainable rank-based p value to 1/12–1/48.


### Does space substitute for time? Concordance of temperature responses

If the alleles that are more common at warmer sites are favoured by warm conditions, they should also rise after warm periods and fall after cool ones within sites. For every SNP, two temperature slopes were estimated with the same binomial GLM and calibrated weights as above: a **spatial** slope (frequency against each site's long-term MUR SST, with a site's seasonal samples pooled) and a **seasonal** slope (the temperature model above: frequency against site + temperature before collection). Their agreement across the genome was measured as the correlation of the two z-scores, and, among the 1% and 5% of SNPs with the strongest spatial slopes, as the fraction whose seasonal slope has the same sign (0.5 = no agreement). The null keeps the spatial slopes and permutes temperatures among each site's sampling events (as in the seasonal test); a second, smaller null permutes site temperatures among sites. This is the genomic counterpart of the within- vs between-site comparison for CTmax (Section 4) and follows the seasonal–clinal comparison of [Machado et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.67577).

Clade X (ME, TK, RW; one lineage, three seasonal sites) is the main test. In clade F the warm sites (MR, FH) and the cool sites (MD, GW) belong to different lineages, so its spatial slopes mostly reflect lineage differences, not temperature; F is shown for completeness but not interpreted. Clade S has one seasonal site, so its seasonal null has a single alternative ordering.

```{r}
#| label: concordance
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
conc_files <- Sys.glob(cx("results", "14_concordance", "*.perm.tsv"))
if (length(conc_files) == 0) {
  cat("Concordance results are not in this export yet.")
} else {
  conc <- map_dfr(conc_files, function(f) {
    read_tsv(f, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(clade = str_split_1(basename(f), "\\.")[1], snps_used = str_split_1(basename(f), "\\.")[2])
  }) %>%
    mutate(snp_set = if_else(snp_set == "all", "all chr.", "no chr6"),
           clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades),
           observed = null == "seasonal" & perm == 0)

  conc %>%
    filter(snp_set == "all chr.", null == "seasonal") %>%
    select(clade, snps_used, observed, r, conc_top1, conc_top5) %>%
    pivot_longer(c(r, conc_top1, conc_top5), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(statistic = recode(statistic, r = "Correlation of z-scores",
                              conc_top1 = "Same direction, top 1% spatial SNPs",
                              conc_top5 = "Same direction, top 5% spatial SNPs"),
           x = paste(clade, snps_used, sep = "\n")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value)) +
    geom_hline(data = tibble(statistic = c("Correlation of z-scores", "Same direction, top 1% spatial SNPs",
                                           "Same direction, top 5% spatial SNPs"), h = c(0, 0.5, 0.5)),
               aes(yintercept = h), colour = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, !observed), colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.7,
               position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, observed), aes(colour = str_sub(x, 1, 1)), size = 3.5, shape = 18) +
    facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(clade_cols[c("F", "S", "X")], c("F", "S", "X")), guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
         caption = "Diamonds: observed. Grey: seasonal null (temperatures permuted among each site's sampling events). All chromosomes.") +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 11)
}
```

```{r}
  conc %>%
    filter(null == "seasonal") %>%
    group_by(clade, snps_used, snp_set) %>%
    summarise(snps = snps[observed],
              r_obs = r[observed], r_rank = sum(r[!observed] >= r[observed]) + 1,
              top1_obs = conc_top1[observed], top1_rank = sum(conc_top1[!observed] >= conc_top1[observed]) + 1,
              top5_obs = conc_top5[observed], top5_rank = sum(conc_top5[!observed] >= conc_top5[observed]) + 1,

    mutate(across(ends_with("_rank"), ~ paste0(.x, " / ", sets))) %>%
    select(-sets) %>%
    arrange(clade, snps_used, snp_set) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3,
                 col.names = c("Clade", "SNPs", "Chromosomes", "SNPs tested", "r", "Rank",

                 caption = "Concordance of spatial and seasonal temperature slopes. Rank = position of the observed value among all seasonal-null orderings (1 = higher than every permutation).")
}
```

In clade X the spatial and seasonal responses point weakly in the same direction: across all SNPs the two slopes are slightly positively correlated (r ≈ 0.04), and among the 1% of SNPs with the strongest spatial slopes about 55% change in the same direction through the season. But the real temperatures rank only 5th–6th of 24 orderings (p ≈ 0.2), 8th–12th on the unlinked set, and the smaller spatial null (6 orderings) cannot go below p ≈ 0.17; removing chromosome 6 changes nothing. So there is no detectable genome-wide concordance between spatial and seasonal temperature responses. Two limits shape this answer. First, the spatial temperature contrast within X is short (7.1–9.9 °C long-term mean across ME, TK and RW), and the spatial slope is mostly ME against the two Gulf of St. Lawrence sites, so it also carries their geographic separation. Second, the null rests on only 24 orderings. A modest true concordance, of the size seen here, could go undetected. Clade F shows the opposite tendency (its observed concordance is the lowest of 48 orderings for the top-1% statistic), but because its spatial contrast is a contrast between lineages (Florida lineages vs F-N) it is not interpreted as a temperature response. Clade S has no usable seasonal null.

In contrast to CTmax, whose between-site slope matches the within-site (acclimation) slope (Section 4), allele frequencies give no evidence that the response to temperature across sites predicts the response through the season. The genomic side of the space-for-time question therefore remains unresolved rather than negative: the data are consistent with no shared response and with a weak one.


## 4. Clade-specific physiological patterns

### CTmax model

To more formally test the relationships between CTmax, collection temperature, and size, we used a linear mixed effects model, structured as `ctmax ~ clade * temp_cent + size + (1 + temp_cent|site) + (1|tube)`. This examines the effects of clade, temperature and size on CTmax, along with clade-specific effects of temperature. Collection temperature was centered before model fitting. The model also includes random intercepts for each site and the tube number (the position of each individual within the water bath during the CTmax assay).

```{r}
#| label: ctmax-model
#| include: false
filtered_data = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  drop_na(size, ctmax) %>% 
  mutate(ctmax_cent = scale(ctmax, scale = F)[,1],
         temp_cent = scale(collection_temp, scale = F)[,1],
         size_cent = scale(size, scale = F)[,1],
         sal_cent = scale(collection_salinity, scale = F)[,1],
         sal_type = if_else(collection_salinity > 15, "High", "Low"), 
         replicate = factor(replicate))

ctmax.model = lme4::lmer(data = filtered_data, 
                         ctmax ~ clade * temp_cent + size + (1 | site) + (1 | replicate) + (1|tube))

performance::check_model(ctmax.model)

lmerTest::ranova(ctmax.model)
car::Anova(ctmax.model, type = "III")

```

### Acclimation vs. site differences (within- and between-site temperature)

A single temperature slope mixes two processes. Within a site, CTmax changes across the season as the same population experiences warmer or cooler water, which is mostly acclimation. Between sites, CTmax differs with each site's typical temperature, which reflects acclimation plus any local adaptation. Collection temperature was therefore split into a within-site component (collection temperature minus the site's mean collection temperature, so it averages zero at every site) and a between-site component (the site's mean temperature minus the mean across sites) ([van de Pol & Wright 2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anbehav.2008.11.006)). If the between-site slope equals the within-site slope, site differences are explained by acclimation to different temperatures; a steeper between-site slope indicates local adaptation on top of plasticity, and a shallower one countergradient variation. Clade is in the model, so turnover of lineages along the coast does not inflate the between-site slope. Body size and the assay terms are kept as in the CTmax model above.

The site mean is currently the mean of each site's collection temperatures. Sites were not sampled in the same seasons (MR and FH only at peak and late), so this will be replaced by the long-term MUR SST climatology (`Output_data/site_climatology.csv`) once it is available; the within-site component stays centred on the collection temperatures.

```{r}
#| label: within-between-model
wb_clim_file <- here("Output", "Output_data", "site_climatology.csv")
wb_events <- filtered_data %>%
  distinct(site, site_code, season, collection_temp) %>%
  group_by(site, site_code) %>%
  summarise(site_mean_collection = mean(collection_temp), .groups = "drop")
if (file.exists(wb_clim_file)) {
  wb_events <- wb_events %>%
    left_join(read_csv(wb_clim_file, show_col_types = FALSE) %>% select(site_code, site_temp = temp_mean),
              by = "site_code")
  wb_source <- "long-term MUR SST mean"
} else {
  wb_events <- mutate(wb_events, site_temp = site_mean_collection)
  wb_source <- "mean of the site's collection temperatures"
}
wb_data <- filtered_data %>%
  left_join(wb_events, by = c("site", "site_code")) %>%
  mutate(t_within = collection_temp - site_mean_collection,
         t_between = site_temp - mean(wb_events$site_temp))

# overall slopes (clade as intercept only) and clade-specific slopes
wb_add <- lme4::lmer(ctmax ~ clade + t_within + t_between + size +
                       (1 | site) + (1 | replicate) + (1 | tube), data = wb_data)
wb_int <- lme4::lmer(ctmax ~ clade * (t_within + t_between) + size +
                       (1 | site) + (1 | replicate) + (1 | tube), data = wb_data)

b <- lme4::fixef(wb_add); V <- as.matrix(vcov(wb_add))
diff_est <- b[["t_between"]] - b[["t_within"]]
diff_se <- sqrt(V["t_between", "t_between"] + V["t_within", "t_within"] - 2 * V["t_between", "t_within"])
wb_overall <- tibble(
  term = c("Within site (acclimation)", "Between sites", "Between − within"),
  slope = c(b[["t_within"]], b[["t_between"]], diff_est),
  se = c(sqrt(V["t_within", "t_within"]), sqrt(V["t_between", "t_between"]), diff_se)) %>%
  mutate(lo = slope - 1.96 * se, hi = slope + 1.96 * se)

wb_clade <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(emmeans::emtrends(wb_int, ~ clade, var = "t_within")) %>%
    transmute(clade, component = "Within site", slope = t_within.trend, lo = lower.CL, hi = upper.CL),
  as_tibble(emmeans::emtrends(wb_int, ~ clade, var = "t_between")) %>%
    transmute(clade, component = "Between sites", slope = t_between.trend, lo = lower.CL, hi = upper.CL)) %>%
  left_join(wb_data %>% group_by(clade) %>% summarise(sites = n_distinct(site), n = n()), by = "clade")

knitr::kable(wb_overall, digits = 3,
             caption = paste0("CTmax slopes (°C per °C) for within-site and between-site temperature, all clades (site temperature: ",
                              wb_source, "). 95% CI = ± 1.96 SE."))
```

```{r}
#| label: within-between-clade-table
wb_clade %>%
  mutate(`Slope (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", slope, lo, hi)) %>%
  select(Clade = clade, Component = component, `Slope (95% CI)`, Sites = sites, Individuals = n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Component, values_from = `Slope (95% CI)`) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Clade-specific CTmax slopes. Between-site slopes rest on few sites per clade and are imprecise.")
```

```{r}
#| label: within-between-plot
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
size_mean <- mean(wb_data$size)
# (A) within site: each site's fitted CTmax across its own collection temperatures
wb_within_lines <- wb_data %>%
  reframe(t_within = range(t_within), .by = c(clade, site, site_code, site_mean_collection, t_between)) %>%
  mutate(size = size_mean, temp = site_mean_collection + t_within)
wb_within_lines$fit <- predict(wb_int, newdata = wb_within_lines, re.form = ~ (1 | site))

p_within <- ggplot(wb_data, aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = wb_within_lines, aes(x = temp, y = fit, colour = site, group = site), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ clade, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) +
  labs(x = "Collection temperature (°C)", y = "CTmax (°C)", colour = "Site",
       title = "A. Within sites (acclimation)") +
  theme_matt_facets(base_size = 12)

# (B) between sites: each site's CTmax at its own mean collection conditions (no within-site
# deviation; fixed effects + site effect) against the site temperature, with the fitted
# between-site slope
wb_site_pts <- wb_data %>%
  distinct(clade, site, site_code, site_mean_collection, site_temp, t_between) %>%
  mutate(t_within = 0, size = size_mean)
wb_site_pts$fit <- predict(wb_int, newdata = wb_site_pts, re.form = ~ (1 | site))
wb_between_line <- wb_site_pts %>%
  reframe(t_between = seq(min(t_between), max(t_between), length.out = 20), .by = clade) %>%
  mutate(t_within = 0, size = size_mean, site_temp = t_between + mean(wb_events$site_temp))
wb_between_line$fit <- predict(wb_int, newdata = wb_between_line, re.form = NA)

p_between <- ggplot(wb_site_pts, aes(x = site_temp, y = fit)) +
  geom_line(data = wb_between_line, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ clade, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) +
  labs(x = paste0("Site temperature (°C; ", wb_source, ")"), y = "Site CTmax (°C)", colour = "Site",
       title = "B. Between sites",
       caption = "B: each site's fitted CTmax at its mean collection conditions; line = between-site slope.") +
  theme_matt_facets(base_size = 12)

ggarrange(p_within, p_between, ncol = 1, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right")
```

CTmax rises by `r sprintf("%.2f", wb_overall$slope[1])` °C for every 1 °C of within-site temperature change (95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", wb_overall$lo[1], wb_overall$hi[1])`), with clade-specific acclimation slopes of `r sprintf("%.2f", min(wb_clade$slope[wb_clade$component == "Within site"]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(wb_clade$slope[wb_clade$component == "Within site"]))`. The between-site slope is `r sprintf("%.2f", wb_overall$slope[2])` (CI `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", wb_overall$lo[2], wb_overall$hi[2])`; site temperature: `r wb_source`), and the difference between the two is `r sprintf("%.2f", wb_overall$slope[3])` (CI `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", wb_overall$lo[3], wb_overall$hi[3])`). If that interval includes zero, CTmax differences between sites within a clade are consistent with acclimation to each site's temperature, with no detectable local adaptation beyond it; with only 2–6 sites per clade, the test can rule out only large differences between the slopes. Panel B shows the site-level pattern behind the between-site slope: each point is a site's CTmax at its own mean collection conditions.


The Stage 1 clade calls (Section 3.1) were merged with the CTmax and body size data set to examine clade-specific patterns of divergence. By plotting CTmax and size against the collection temperature we can see that these clades appear to be physiologically differentiated. Clades F and S tend to have higher CTmax, even when collected at the same temperatures as Clades X and IV. Size is more variable, with varying degrees of temperature sensitivity across the clades. Overall, however, Clade F tends to be smaller than Clades S and X. Clade IV tended to be the largest.

The general result here is that Clade F appears to be more thermally tolerant than Clades S and X, which in turn are more thermally tolerant than Clade IV. Clade IV does however, appear to exibit stronger plasticity than the other clades (although this pattern is only marginally significant in two of the comparisons; IV-S and IV-X)

These differences in physiology correspond to the distributional patterns for each clade. Using a Loess smoother (span = 2) highlights how the proportional abundance of the clades is affected by temperature in different ways. Clade F occurs in high proportion at high temperature, Clade IV occurs in high proportions at low temperatures, while Clade X occurs in high proportions at intermediate temperatures. Clade S generally occurs in low proportions, with a few exceptions.

### Trait variability within clades

Shown below is the trait variation (ranges) for each site. Ranges are calculated for each collection separately.

```{r}

#| fig-height: 4.5

  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  group_by(site, season, clade, collection_temp, collection_salinity, doy, lat) %>% 
  summarise(mean_ctmax = mean(ctmax),
            ctmax_range = max(ctmax) - min(ctmax),
            ctmax_var = var(ctmax),
            mean_size = mean(size),
            size_range = max(size) - min(size),
            size_var = var(size)) %>% 
  mutate(prop_ctmax_range = ctmax_range / mean_ctmax,
         prop_size_range = size_range / mean_size)

ctmax_range_temp = ggplot(trait_ranges, aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax_range)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) +

ggarrange(ctmax_var_temp, size_var_temp, common.legend = T, legend = "right")
```

Changes in trait variance may be indicative of phenotypic selection. If selection (as opposed to acclimation) are driving seasonal changes, we may expect to see a reduction in variance in the peak samples relative to the early season samples. Note that early season collection temperatures this year were higher than expected, driven by fairly strong heatwaves across the North Atlantic. As shown in the temperature profiles for each site, the 'early' samples were collected just after high temperatures were reached, while 'peak' samples were collected after sites had experienced high temperatures for several weeks (generations). As warming tolerances were fairly high throughout this period, we will assume that selection was weak before the early samples. If the early onset of high temperatures filtered out vulnerable genotypes prior to our sampling, the results will be a conservative estimate of the effects of selection on trait variance.

### Parasites, epibionts and thermal limits

Infected and uninfected individuals are compared within the same collection (same site, date and collection temperature), so differences are not confounded with acclimation temperature. Only collections with at least two positive and two negative individuals are shown.

```{r}
#| label: infection-traits
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
inf_groups <- c(paradinium = "Paradinium", trematode = "Trematodes",
                apostome = "Apostome ciliates", peritrich = "Peritrich ciliates")
inf <- join_data %>%
  select(sample_id, site_code, season, clade, ctmax, size, paste0(names(inf_groups), "_call")) %>%
  pivot_longer(ends_with("_call"), names_to = "group", values_to = "positive",
               names_pattern = "(.*)_call") %>%
  mutate(collection = paste(site_code, season)) %>%
  group_by(group, collection) %>%
  filter(sum(positive) >= 2, sum(!positive) >= 2) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(group = factor(inf_groups[group], levels = inf_groups),
         status = factor(if_else(positive, "positive", "negative"), levels = c("negative", "positive")))

if (nrow(inf) == 0) {
  cat("No collection has both infected and uninfected individuals.")
} else {
  inf %>%
    pivot_longer(c(ctmax, size), names_to = "trait") %>%
    mutate(trait = recode(trait, ctmax = "CTmax (°C)", size = "Prosome length (mm)")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = collection, y = value, colour = status)) +
    facet_grid(trait ~ group, scales = "free", space = "free_x",
               labeller = labeller(group = label_wrap_gen(12))) +
    geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
               size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 10,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(negative = "grey65", positive = "grey10")) +
    labs(x = "Collection (site, season)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: infection-models
infection_fit <- function(var) {
  d <- join_data %>%
    mutate(collection = paste(site_code, season), status = .data[[var]]) %>%
    group_by(collection) %>% filter(any(status), any(!status)) %>% ungroup()
  if (nrow(d) == 0) return(NULL)
  map_dfr(c("ctmax", "size"), function(tr) {
    m <- lme4::lmer(as.formula(paste(tr, "~ status + clade + (1 | collection)")), data = d)
    co <- summary(m)$coefficients["statusTRUE", ]
    tibble(covariate = var, trait = tr, n_collections = n_distinct(d$collection),
           n_positive = sum(d$status), effect = co[["Estimate"]], se = co[["Std. Error"]])
  })
}
bind_rows(infection_fit("parasite_any"), infection_fit("epibiont_any")) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Effect of carrying a parasite or epibiont on CTmax and size, within collections (trait ~ status + clade + (1 | collection)); only collections with both positive and negative individuals.")
```

## 5. Partitioning vulnerability

Our study examines spatial and temporal variation in upper thermal limits for field-acclimated individuals. Given the short generation time of these copepods, our results likely reflect the combined influence of phenotypic plasticity (acclimation to the changes in temperature), local adaptation (variation amongst the sites), and genetic variation between the clades.

The four clades, while morphologically difficult to differentiate, have distinct geographic distributions and physiological tolerances. The inclusion of this clade-level variation decreases the slope of the CTmax vs. temperature regression. Ignoring this source of variation would lead to an overestimated capacity for *A. tonsa* to respond to warming (either through acclimation or via gene flow and evolutionary rescue).

```{r}
#| label: clade-trait-lat
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
join_data %>% 
  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax, colour = clade)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(data = filter(join_data, clade != "A_hudsonica"),
              method = "lm", linewidth = 2.5, 
              colour = "black") + 
  labs(x = "Collection Temp. (°C)", 
       y = "CTmax (°C)") + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = clade_cols) + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

We illustrate the effects of these different levels of variation by calculating warming tolerance for each collection (site x collection temperature combination) under three different scenarios.

### Scenario 1 (Fixed CTmax)

Warming tolerance was calculated using the average CTmax from the peak season collections (across all sites and individuals regardless of clade). This essentially assumes a fixed CTmax that is constant across the geographic range examined.

```{r}
illus_data = join_data %>% 
  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica")

peak_mean = illus_data %>% 
  filter(season == "peak") %>% 
  summarise(mean = mean(ctmax))

mean_ctmax = peak_mean$mean[1]

mean_ctmax_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("pred_wt" = mean_ctmax - temp_c) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Fixed CTmax") %>%  
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

```

### Scenario 2 (Clade-level variation)

Here, the same approach is taken but for each clade separately. The average CTmax from the peak season for each clade was used as a fixed CTmax value when calculating warming tolerance.

```{r}

clade_peak_mean = illus_data %>% 
  filter(season == "peak") %>% 
  group_by(clade) %>% 
  summarise(mean = mean(ctmax))


clade_mean_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Clade") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(clade_mean_profiles, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(clade_mean_profiles$pred_wt))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

### Scenario 3 (Clade variation and acclimation/adaptation)

Here CTmax is predicted based on the continuous temperature data and a model of CTmax as a function of the interaction between collection temperature and clade. The predicted CTmax values fall within the range of CTmax values observed in the field.

```{r}

pred.model = lm(data = illus_data, ctmax ~ collection_temp * clade)

pred_data = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>%  
  select(region, doy, date, "collection_temp" = temp_c, clade)


pred_data$pred_ctmax = predict(pred.model, newdata = pred_data)

full_pred_profiles = pred_data %>% 
  mutate(pred_wt = pred_ctmax - collection_temp) %>% 
  select(region, doy, date, "temp_c" = collection_temp, -pred_ctmax, clade, pred_wt) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Genetic Variation & Acclimation") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(full_pred_profiles, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(full_pred_profiles$pred_wt))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

### Comparing Scenarios

There is strong geographic variation in the distributions of these clades. It does not, for example, make sense to examine warming tolerance of Clade X individuals in Florida, as this clade was not collected from lower latitudes. To incorporate this distribution information, simulated populations were re-assembled reflecting the proportional clade composition within each region (calculated across the entire set of collections).

```{r}
#| label: region-clade-props
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
# First step is to generate a population of 100 individuals for each region reflecting the number of individuals in each clade 

pred_samples = illus_data %>%  
  mutate(region = case_when(
    site_code %in% c("MR", "FH") ~ "Florida",
    site_code %in% c("GW", "MD") ~ "Chesapeake",
    site_code == "CT" ~ "Connecticut",
    site_code == "ME" ~ "Maine",
    site_code == "TK" ~ "Shediac",
    site_code == "RW" ~ "Miramichi"
  )) %>% 
  group_by(region) %>%  
  count(clade) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  complete(region, clade, fill = list(n = 0)) %>% 
  group_by(region) %>% 
  mutate(total = sum(n)) %>% 
  group_by(region, clade) %>% 
  mutate(prop = n / total, 
         sample_size = round(prop * 100)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake","Connecticut", "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(mutate(pred_samples, clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)), aes(x = region, y = prop, fill = clade)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Region", 
       y = "Proportion") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

Warming tolerance profiles for each clade were added in these proportions to generation populations of 100 individuals.

```{r}
clade_mean_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = clade_mean_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "no")
  
  clade_mean_populations = bind_rows(clade_mean_populations, new_df)
  
}

full_pred_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = full_pred_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "no")
  
  full_pred_populations = bind_rows(full_pred_populations, new_df)
  
}

```

The warming tolerance distributions for each region and the three different scenarios are shown below.

Overall, differences were fairly minor, with slight increases in predicted warming tolerance in low latitude regions and slight decreases in higher latitude regions.

We also examined potential effects of warming (a +4°C increase in temperature). These predictions assume clade composition does not change over time and that warming is constant throughout the year.

```{r}

warming_clade_mean_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  mutate(temp_c = temp_c + 4) %>%

         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>%

               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Clade") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

warming_clade_mean_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]

}


warming_pred_data = temp_profiles %>% 
  mutate(temp_c = temp_c + 4) %>%

  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,

warming_pred_data$pred_ctmax = predict(pred.model, newdata = warming_pred_data)

warming_full_pred_profiles = warming_pred_data %>%
```

Unsurprisingly warming decreases the predicted warming tolerance. Similar patterns are observed as in the comparison between the initial three scenarios - predicted warming tolerance under warming is lowest in Florida and highest in the high latitude regions. Similarly, including clade-level variation and acclimation increases warming tolerance in the lower latitude regions and decreases it in the higher latitude regions.

To simplify the comparisons, here we subset the data to just August and September (the warmest months and the season typically associated with the highest abundance of A. tonsa).

```{r}
#| label: wt-range-scenarios
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

wt_comps = bind_rows(mean_ctmax_profiles %>% 
  mutate(warming = "no") %>% 
  bind_rows(warming_mean_ctmax_profiles),
clade_mean_populations, 
warming_clade_mean_populations, 
full_pred_populations, 
warming_full_pred_populations) %>% 
  group_by(region, comparison, warming) %>% 
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(pred_wt),
            min_wt = min(pred_wt),
            max_wt = max(pred_wt)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(comparison = fct_relevel(comparison, "Fixed CTmax", "Genetic Variation", "Genetic Variation & Acclimation"))

peak_comps = bind_rows(mean_ctmax_profiles %>% 
  mutate(warming = "no") %>% 
  bind_rows(warming_mean_ctmax_profiles),
clade_mean_populations, 
warming_clade_mean_populations, 
full_pred_populations, 
warming_full_pred_populations) %>% 
  mutate("month" = month(date)) %>% 
  filter(month %in% c(8,9)) %>%  
  group_by(region, comparison, warming) %>% 
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(pred_wt),
            min_wt = min(pred_wt),
            max_wt = max(pred_wt)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(comparison = fct_relevel(comparison, "Fixed CTmax", "Genetic Variation", "Genetic Variation & Acclimation"))

ggplot(peak_comps, aes(x = comparison, y = mean_wt, colour = warming, group = warming))+ 
  facet_wrap(region~., 
             nrow = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + 
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = min_wt, ymax = max_wt),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.3),
                width = 0.1, linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("no" = "darkslategray", 
                                 "yes" = "darksalmon")) + 
  labs(x = "", 
       y = "Warming Tolerance (°C)") + 
  theme_matt_facets() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 300, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5))

```

Changes were slight between the scenarios, with the same relative patterns between the current and warming scenarios. Compared to the fixed CTmax estimate, incorporating both genetic diversity and acclimation reduced the range of warming tolerance estimates across the samples by \~30%.

```{r}

range_changes = wt_comps %>%  
  filter(warming == "no") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(warming, comparison) %>% 
  summarise(wt_range = max(min_wt) - min(min_wt)) %>% 
  mutate(percent_decrease = 100 * (1 - (wt_range / wt_range[1]))) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  select("Comparison" = comparison, "WT Range" = wt_range, "% Decrease" = percent_decrease) %>% 
  arrange(`% Decrease`)
 
# Saved for the phenotype manuscript (Table 2)
write.csv(range_changes, file = here("Output", "Output_data", "range_changes.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(range_changes, digits = 2)

```
